dataset.name: Arctic shrub and Eriophorum leaf and root decomposition, northern Alaska, 2017-2018
description: This data package contains litter decomposition data collected from 170 plots of rapidly expanding shrub genera (Alnus, Betula, and Salix) and a widespread sedge (Eriophorum vaginatum) along a latitudinal and temperature gradient in northern Alaska. These data were produced from a litter bag experiment that took place from July 2017 to July 2018 and include mass loss and nitrogen loss decomposition metrics for both leaf and root litters. These raw data support a submitted manuscript that examines the variability in decomposition between shrub and graminoid leaf and root litters across a 1-year experiment across the graminoid-dominated Arctic tundra and reveals how deciduous shrub expansion affects litter decomposition in tundra ecosystems. Data are presented by site (n=5) and patch (shrub or sedge plot) in csv files. The site and plot location data and environmental measurement data are provided in Fraterrigo and Chen (2020). Additional methods regarding plot distribution and environmental measurements are in Chen et al. (2020) and Fraterrigo et al. (2024).

measurementTechnique:
Environmental data
We obtained downscaled (1 km) monthly mean precipitation and temperature data from the Climate Research Unit data (CRU TS4.05 datasets; Harris et al., 2020) that overlapped with the duration of the decomposition experiment (June 2017-July 2018). Precipitation and temperature data were summarized into three categories: mean annual, mean summer (June-August), and mean winter (December-February).
Microenvironmental data and in-depth methodology are available in Fraterrigo and Chen (2023) and Fraterrigo et al. (2024),respectively.

Litter decomposition
All litter used in the decomposition experiment was collected near Fairbanks, AK, during the spring of 2017. Eriophorum vaginatum litter along with Alnus rubra, Betula glandulosa, Betula occidentalis, Salix lasiandra, Salix bebbiana, and Salix alaxensis were collected to represent the genera of interest. The litter was collected from at least six plots of each species and pooled by genus to ensure an adequate representation of generic litter variability. All the sampled root or leaf materials of the same genus were well mixed to maximize the litter quantity and to ensure that litter bags received homogeneous litter samples. Senesced leaf litter was collected directly from plants and supplemented with senesced leaves from the topmost litter layer (0-1 cm depth) if additional material was needed.
Shrub root material was collected by cutting the main root branches connected to the plants of the target species. Sedge (Eriophorum) root material was collected directly below the tussock. Previously dead root material was removed. All roots were rinsed and both leaf and root materials were oven dried at 55 ° C for 24 hours and then sent to the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.
In the laboratory, absorptive roots (1st-3rd orders) were carefully dissected from the shrub root branches. For sedge roots that do not have a branching architecture, all individual root segments were considered absorptive roots.
A subsample of litter from each genus was ground and analyzed using a Costech Elemental Analyzer to determine the initial C and N values.
Litter bags were assembled with oven-dried leaves and absorptive roots. Litter bags were constructed of 0.5 mm diameter vinyl coated polyester mesh sewn into 10 x 10 cm pouches. We prepared separate leaf and root bags; leaf litter bags contained material from a single genus and were packed with 1.0 g of senesced leaf material and root bags were packed with 0.5 g of excised absorptive root material. The use of uniformly sized mesh throughout the experiment allowed us to quantify differences caused by variables of interest within the design. Litter bags were deployed in late June and early July 2017.
A total of 677 litter bags were deployed across the five study sites to evaluate factors that regulate litter decomposition. Leaf bags were placed horizontally on the substrate surface and root bags vertically at a depth of 0-10 cm. In July 2018, 657 litter bags were recovered and returned to Illinois for analysis; twenty of the initially deployed bags could not be relocated in the field.
The litter was cleaned of foreign materials, oven dried at 55 ° C for 48 hours, and then weighed to determine the mass loss. Subsamples of dried decomposed litter from each litter bag were ground and C and N percentages were analyzed with a Costech Elemental Analyzer. These values may exceed 100% due to N immobilization or N fixation occurring in the litter substrate.
